titleStmt.title: Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the White House

div.head: 450. Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State and the White House
div.p: Secto 4032. Subject: Memorandum for the President: My talks with the Uruguayan leaders.
4. Subject: My talks with the Uruguayan leaders.
5. In three separate sessions in Montevideo this morning I met with the Vice President and Congressional leaders, the new economic team, and the Foreign Minister.

6. All seem to be over their post inauguration euphoria. Justifiably proud of their return to democracy, they are sobered by the difficulties of making it work in the face of serious economic deterioration. The Finance Minister impressed me with his very persuasive recitation of the current situation, and the long downhill slide Uruguay has seen in the last ten years. The GDP has declined 15 percent in the last three years and real wages are one-half of ten years ago. Uruguay was an early leader in establishing a welfare state. The Uruguayan leadership recognizes that it has a lot of internal housekeeping to do and (a refreshing change) that direct foreign capital investment (as opposed to loans) is the needed ingredient to invoke growth. Good intentions notwithstanding, they have a significant challenge ahead.
7. The Foreign Minister appears as capable as the Finance Minister but in a more open, effusive way. He’s well schooled in the international economic arena and I think they’ll be a strong team.

8. In summary, in my initial evaluation of the new government I count as pluses their aim to see direct foreign investment as a needed boost, a capable foreign policy and financial team, and a generally moderate albeit independent
foreign policy. Among the minuses, the hint that Sanguinetti likes to appeal to leftist elements among his constituencies and the attendant dangers of posturing being turned into policy, as in the recognition of Cuba, announced the day of the inaugural.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, N850003–0271. Secret; Immediate; Nodis. Sent from aboard the Delegation’s aircraft.

In telegram 1171 from Montevideo, March 2, the Embassy reported on Shultz’s March 2 breakfast meeting with Uruguayan Vice President Enrique Tarigo and Senators Jorge Batlle (Colorado Party) and Luis Alberto Lacalle (Blanco Party). (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850144–0091) In telegram 1172 from Montevideo, March 2, the Embassy reported on Shultz’s March 2 meeting with Sanguinetti’s new economic team. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850144–0095) In telegram 1170 from Montevideo, March 2, the Embassy reported on Shultz’s March 2 meeting with Iglesias during which they “agreed that sound economic policies were the key to Uruguay’s economic recovery.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850144–0089)

Under cover of a March 6 memorandum to McFarlane, Tillman sent a report on her trip to Sanguinetti’s inauguration noting, “that the Sandinistas had done excellent advance work” to ensure a warm welcome for Ortega while “we, in turn, were frequently greeted with chants of ‘yanqui asesino’ (yankee assassins) and ‘no pasaran’ (they won’t get through), a favorite Sandinista war chant. It helped underscore the well-organized left which confronts Sanguinetti. However, the staged nature of the demonstrations against us became clear as we left to go to the airport. Seeing the U.S. flag on the limo, ordinary Uruguayans, on the beach, on the streets, stood to applaud and wave at us. Their friendliness was heartening.” (Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Subject File, Uruguay)
